## Trusted Resources

## Official legal help resources

If you need free or low-cost legal help, these official resources can point you to licensed attorneys and legal aid in your state.

- USA.gov — Find a lawyer for affordable legal aid (https://www.usa.gov/legal-aid): Programs and organizations that give free legal advice and may help you find a free or low-cost attorney.
- Legal Services Corporation — I Need Legal Help (https://www.lsc.gov/about-lsc/what-legal-aid/get-legal-help): Find legal aid in your community for people with low incomes.
- LawHelp.org (https://www.lawhelp.org/): Find free legal aid near you and get answers to your legal questions.
- ABA Free Legal Answers (https://abafreelegalanswers.org/): This site lets people with low incomes ask questions online and have a lawyer answer them. They will not answer questions involving crimes.

## Guide: What to Expect at Your First Consultation with an Attorney

28 October 2026

Please note: this guide is general information only — it is not legal advice, and it does not create an attorney-client relationship. Consultation practices vary by attorney, firm, and state, and only a licensed attorney in your state can advise you on your specific situation.

A first consultation is a conversation, not a commitment. Its purpose is for you and the attorney to learn enough about each other to decide whether working together makes sense. Knowing what usually happens in that meeting — and what to bring and ask — helps you get real value out of it.

### 1. What a consultation usually covers

Most consultations follow a similar shape. The attorney will ask you to explain your situation in your own words: what happened, when, and what outcome you are hoping for. They will ask follow-up questions about dates, documents, and anyone else involved. Then they will usually explain, in general terms, how matters like yours are typically handled, what the main steps would be, and what the realistic range of outcomes looks like. Be wary of anyone who guarantees a specific result — no attorney can promise how a case will end.

The meeting is also your chance to judge the attorney. Notice whether they listen, explain things in plain language, and answer your questions directly, or whether they rush you, dodge questions, or pressure you to sign something on the spot.

### 2. What to bring

Bring anything that helps the attorney understand your situation quickly. Useful items often include:

— Any letters, contracts, notices, or court papers related to the matter
— A short written timeline: key dates and what happened on each
— Names and contact details of other people involved, where relevant
— Any deadlines you already know about
— A list of your own questions, so you do not forget them in the meeting

You do not need to organise everything perfectly. A clear, honest account matters more than a polished file — but do not leave out facts that hurt your side. An attorney can only advise you well on the full picture, and surprises discovered later can damage your matter.

### 3. How fees are usually discussed

Fees should be discussed openly at the first meeting, before any work begins. Attorneys commonly charge in one of a few ways: an hourly rate, a flat fee for a defined piece of work, or — in some kinds of cases — a contingency arrangement where the fee depends on the outcome. Ask which model applies to your matter, what it covers, what it does not cover, and what other costs (such as filing fees or expert costs) might arise separately.

Whatever is agreed should be put in writing in a fee agreement before work starts. If the fee structure is unclear, or you are asked to pay a large sum in cash with no written agreement, treat that as a warning sign and consider a second opinion.

### 4. Questions worth asking

— Have you handled matters like mine before, and what happened in general terms?
— What are the realistic options, and what are the risks of each?
— How long do matters like this usually take?
— Who will actually do the work — you, or someone else in the firm?
— How will we communicate, and how quickly should I expect replies?
— What will this cost, and what could change that estimate?

A straightforward attorney will answer these plainly. Evasiveness about experience, fees, or who does the work is itself useful information.

### 5. After the consultation

You are not obliged to hire the first attorney you meet. Take time to compare: how clearly did they explain your options, did the fee arrangement make sense, and did you feel heard? If something felt wrong — pressure to sign immediately, a guaranteed outcome, or an unwillingness to put fees in writing — those are good reasons to consult someone else.

If you do decide to proceed, confirm the agreement in writing, keep copies of everything you sign, and note any deadlines the attorney mentioned. If you decide not to proceed, say so plainly so the attorney does not hold your matter open.

### Quick checklist

— Relevant documents and a short timeline brought to the meeting
— Your questions written down in advance
— Fee model and likely extra costs discussed and understood
— Fee agreement in writing before any work begins
— No guaranteed outcome promised, and no pressure to sign on the spot
— Decision made at your own pace, after comparing options if needed

## Guide: How to Verify an Attorney's License and Disciplinary History Before You Hire

27 October 2026

Please note: this guide is general information only — it is not legal advice, and it does not create an attorney-client relationship. Licensing and disciplinary rules vary by state, and only a licensed attorney in your state can advise you on your specific situation.

Before you hire an attorney, it is worth spending a few minutes confirming two basic things: that the attorney is licensed to practice in your state, and whether any disciplinary action has been taken against them. Both checks are free, and both use public records kept by the state bar association or the state's attorney licensing authority.

### 1. Confirm the attorney is licensed in your state

Attorneys are licensed state by state. An attorney licensed in one state cannot necessarily practise in another, so check the state where your matter will be handled — not just the state where the attorney's office sits.

Every state bar association, or the state's equivalent licensing body, maintains a public directory of licensed attorneys. Search it using the attorney's full name, and confirm that the listing matches the person you are considering: same name, same firm, and a status showing they are currently admitted and in good standing.

### 2. Check the disciplinary record

The same state bar directory usually shows whether an attorney has been disciplined, and often links to the public record of any action. Discipline can range from a private reprimand to suspension or disbarment, and the record normally describes what happened in general terms.

A single old, minor entry does not automatically mean an attorney is a bad choice — but it is something you are entitled to know about, and to ask about. If the record shows a suspension, disbarment, or a pattern of complaints, treat that as a serious warning sign and consider other options.

### 3. Ask the attorney directly

Verification is not only about databases. In your first conversation, it is reasonable to ask:

— Are you licensed in this state, and in good standing with the state bar?
— Have you ever been disciplined, and if so, what happened?
— Have you handled matters like mine before, and what were the realistic outcomes?

A straightforward attorney will answer these questions plainly. Evasiveness about licensing or discipline is itself useful information.

### 4. Watch for warning signs

Be cautious if an attorney will not give you their full name or bar number, pressures you to sign or pay immediately, guarantees a specific outcome, or asks you to pay in cash with no written fee agreement. No attorney can guarantee how a case will end, and fee arrangements should always be put in writing before work begins.

### 5. Keep a record of what you checked

Note the date you checked, the directory you used, and what it showed. If anything about the listing looks inconsistent — a different firm name, a different state, or a status that is not clearly active — ask the attorney to explain it before you proceed, and consider a second opinion.

### Quick checklist

— Attorney's name and firm match the state bar directory listing
— Licensed and in good standing in the state where your matter will be handled
— Disciplinary record checked, and any entries understood
— Direct questions about licensing and discipline answered plainly
— Fee arrangement discussed and put in writing before work begins
